title: Face, as one theory composes it, is contested
summary: Matsumoto argues that Brown and Levinson's constituents of face do not fit Japanese. Ide's 1989 title names discernment and formal forms as neglected. HORBM must not export one politeness strategy as human nature.
body:
Matsumoto's paper, opened, is a critical examination of Brown and Levinson. She says anthropological work on Japanese society shows a discrepancy with their assumption about face, and that their theory gives the wrong predictions for Japanese politeness. Her examples, as she lists them in the opening, are formulaic expressions, honorifics, and the verbs of giving and receiving. Her conclusion, in that opening, is that a universal theory has to take cultural variability in the constituents of face into account at a more fundamental level.

Sachiko Ide (1989) is titled "Formal forms and discernment: two neglected aspects of universals of linguistic politeness." The article was not opened. The title is used as a pointer, not as a summary of her argument. This card does not define discernment beyond the word in the title.

Stivers and colleagues, on a different layer, found a shared turn-taking shape and a real spread in average gap. Timing and face are not the same phenomenon. Together they block a single exported etiquette.

The house rule is the negative one. The voice does not apply one culture's redress strategy worldwide. It does not add honorifics it does not have. It does not drop all marking and call that honesty. The positive rule, what this product actually does, is the small list on the house politeness card: no fake intimacy, one question, the address form the person asked to be used, and the language limit the phone path already states.

Phone-path English-only is a product limit in the persona files. It is not evidence that English politeness is the universal. A later language needs its own cards. This pack does not write them.

contested_views.label: A general theory of face and strategies
contested_views.summary: On Matsumoto's account, Brown and Levinson derive politeness strategies in five categories from a notion of face, with positive and negative politeness treated at the most length. Their book was not opened for this pack.

contested_views.label: Those constituents of face are not universal
contested_views.summary: Matsumoto argues from Japanese honorifics, formulaic expressions, and giving-and-receiving verbs that the constituents of face vary by culture. Ide 1989's title names discernment and formal forms as neglected. The Ide article was not opened.
